references.text: The Lord gives Moses instructions to speak to the children of Israel regarding offerings, a similar introduction to ritual law.
Command to bring an offering to the Lord, using the same term קָרְבָּן (korban/offer).
Abel brought an offering from the flock (צֹאן), mentioned as one of the sources of offerings in Leviticus 1:2.
Noah offered from cattle and sheep on the altar to the Lord, the same types of animals mentioned here.
The Passover lamb was to be taken from the flock or cattle, the same categories of sacrificial animals mentioned in Leviticus 1:2.
Specifies that voluntary offerings must come from cattle, sheep, or goats - expanding on the קָרְבָּן laws.
Refers to offerings from sheep and cattle that are to be brought to the place the Lord chooses.
The Letter to the Hebrews explains that animal sacrifices under the old covenant were a shadow of what was to come, and that blood from bulls and goats could never take away sins.
Paul uses sacrificial terminology (θυσίαν) and urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice.
The general introduction about offerings in Lev 1:2 finds its specific application for the peace offering in Lev 7:29.
Lev 22:18 expands and confirms the principle in Lev 1:2 by including foreigners and specifying the motivations for the offering.
Lev 9:3 is the concrete historical fulfillment of the general requirements for sacrificial animals set forth in Lev 1:2.
Lev 4:2 complements Lev 1:2 by defining the obligation to offer when one has sinned unintentionally, while 1:2 deals with voluntary offerings.
